title: plainly, in one session, as a shape not a checklist
hook: plainly, in one session, as a shape not a checklist
carry: five things that hold a life up

segments.voice: Yesterday: inshallah. If it's meant. A whole plan, held with an open hand. Did the thing you planned turn out the way you pictured? Day five.

Most people learn the five pillars of Islam the way you learn a list for a test. Witness. Prayer. Giving. Fasting. Pilgrimage. Five words, five boxes, done. And if that's all you have, it sounds like a checklist: tick the boxes, pass. But that isn't how the tradition itself pictures them. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ described them as a building. So today, plainly, in one sitting, you get all five, not as a list but as a shape. And the shape turns out to be made of time.
screen: `FIVE WORDS, FIVE BOXES?` → `NOT A CHECKLIST.` → `A BUILDING.`

segments.voice: The hadith is in both Bukhari and Muslim: Islam is built on five. Built, like a house. Pillars are what keep the roof up. One: the shahada, the witness. There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God. One sentence. Said to become Muslim, said inside every prayer, whispered to a newborn, hoped for as a last word. Its clock is always. Two: salat, prayer, five times a day, at times that move with the sun: dawn, midday, afternoon, sunset, night. Many Shia Muslims join them into three sittings; the prayers are still five. Its clock is the day. Three: zakat, giving a share of what you have to people in need, counted once a year; in Sunni practice usually two and a half percent of savings. Four: sawm, fasting from dawn to sunset through the month of Ramadan. Their clock is the year. Five: hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca, once in a lifetime. Its clock is a life. Now look at the shape. Always. Every day. Every year. Once in a life. Circles inside circles, from a single breath out to a whole lifetime. And the house is built to fit the person living in it. The Qur'an lets the sick and the traveler make up missed fast days later, and asks for the hajj only from those able to make the journey. Muslims also draw the house in more than one way. Sunni teaching usually names these five as the pillars. Shia teaching usually speaks of roots, the core beliefs, and branches, the practices. Prayer, fasting, giving and pilgrimage sit among the branches, and the witness lives in the roots. Same house, drawn two ways.
screen: `ISLAM IS BUILT ON FIVE.` · `ALWAYS, DAILY, YEARLY, ONCE.` · `BUILT TO FIT THE PERSON.` · `ROOTS AND BRANCHES: DRAWN TWO WAYS.` · then, large: `FIVE THINGS THAT HOLD A LIFE UP.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. The pillars are circles of time, so let's borrow the shape. First breath: something that holds up your day. Second breath: something that holds up your year. Third breath: something you'd want to do once in your life. You don't have to do anything about them yet. Just see what's holding you up.
The five pillars. Witness, prayer, giving, fasting, pilgrimage. Not five boxes but a house built on five. Fifth word.
Your line: five things that hold a life up. Today, notice one thing you do every day that you'd miss if it fell. Day five.

howItsDone: Muslims keep the five together: the shahada as the core of faith, the five daily prayers, zakat given yearly, the Ramadan fast, and the hajj once in a lifetime for those able. Shia Muslims keep the same practices and describe the faith as roots (beliefs) and branches (practices).

original.note: Arabic: "the pillars of Islam." arkan is the plural of rukn, a pillar or supporting corner.

trapdoor: what you thought: five rules to tick off.
what it means: five practices a life is built on — "Islam is built on five," in a hadith in Bukhari and Muslim.
what a scholar hears: the five run on nested clocks: always (shahada), daily (salat), yearly (zakat, sawm), once in a life (hajj). Shia teaching draws the same house as roots and branches.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 8; Sahih Muslim 16 (Islam is built on five)
Shia teaching: usul al-din and furu' al-din (roots and branches of religion)

notes: Hadith numbers for 'Islam is built on five' (Bukhari 8, Muslim 16) cited from memory; please confirm.

Zakat described as 'in Sunni practice usually two and a half percent of savings' (held a year above the nisab); Shia zakat applies to specific kinds of wealth and Shia Muslims also pay khums. The script keeps this short; confirm it isn't misleading.
Shia description: roots (tawhid, adl, nubuwwa, imama, ma'ad) and branches (salat, sawm, zakat, khums, hajj, and others). The script says the witness 'lives in the roots'; confirm.
Shahada 'whispered to a newborn' refers to the adhan said in a newborn's ear, which contains it; confirm the phrasing.
